content: Hi everyone, does CSLib have a definition of the category of LTSs along with some basic constructions/properties?

:wave:
Yep, here you go: https://api.cslib.io/docs/Cslib/Foundations/Semantics/LTS/Basic.html

We've battle tested it with automata theory, bisimulation/simulation/trace equivalence, CCS, and HML so far. We're currently developing a couple of projects on choreographic programming at FORM with it.

But there's a lot to cover still.
Or did you mean literally category as in category theory?

Fabrizio Montesi said:

Or did you mean literally category as in category theory?

Yes, I meant as in category theory. I have been looking at Winskel and Nielsen’s handbook chapter.

We don't currently, but it seems pretty reasonable to add this. And I think Mathlib has enough about fibred categories for this purpose as well? I have run into universe issues trying this sort of thing for lambda calculi, but maybe this is different for LTSs.

Chris Henson said:

but it seems pretty reasonable to add this.

Great, I would be happy to contribute this to CSLib.
Are we talking about coalgebras and dialgebras?

I'm no category theorist but I've used them, and they're quite relevant for a number of developments. Some people working on semantics at FORM might be looking at them as well, I'd be happy to bridge.

In any case: definitely relevant. :⁠-⁠)
For just the category, it is just LTS as objects and the morphisms are a pair of mappings of states and labels that preserve the transition relation, right?
I see, thanks! :+1:

Chris Henson said:

For just the category, it is just LTS as objects and the morphisms are a pair of mappings of states and labels that preserve the transition relation, right?

Yes, I just need these basics for now.

Thanks for the short and to the point PR, review in progress. :)
@Ayberk Tosun I left a review with some comments about the definitions you have written. If there are questions it is maybe easier to discuss here.
In short, I think you have something analogous to confusing "the category of X" with "X as a category". (Like we have for groups, preorders, etc.)

Fabrizio Montesi said:

Thanks for the short and to the point PR, review in progress. :)

Thanks for the review :slight_smile: I started addressing your comments but I need to change the notion of morphism to be partial as in the handbook chapter. I actually think this is crucial and the current definition is wrong.
To be clear, this should get encoded through dependent typing, yes? Just as is done implicitly in the definition of docs#CategoryTheory.CategoryStruct itself.

@Chris Henson Regarding the other comment: that is indeed right. The category structure should be on $\Sigma S : Type , \Sigma L : Type , LTS S L$. I actually think the definition of LTS is a bit misleading, which tripped me up. I would call the current definition LTS-Structure and I would define LTS := Σ S : Type , Σ L : Type , LTS-Structure S L.

Distinguishing between the structure and the bundled construction this way is quite common in type theory: https://martinescardo.github.io/TypeTopology/Groups.Type.html#3789 , and this is the convention I’m used to :slight_smile:
I will fix this it but I might not have time today

Yes, I see how this could be misleading coming from Agda. (I'm a big HoTT and TypeTopology fan btw!)

The difference I think is that in Lean bundling is rare enough that we don't have a convention like this. Categories are an exception to this.

Ayberk Tosun said:

I will fix this it but I might not have time today

And no worries, take your time!

@Chris Henson: I fixed it now. I defined BundledLTS and defined everything on that. I don’t like the name “bundled LTS” but it is convenient to have a name for it at the moment and I cannot think of a better name. The only better name I can think of is “LTS” which is taken by the transition relation of an LTS.
I’m open to suggestions on naming and so on

It is double dollar signs for LaTeX.

Ayberk Tosun said:

I’m open to suggestions on naming and so on

This comment has examples from Mathlib that I would follow.
@Chris Henson @Fabrizio Montesi I’m sorry I couldn’t respond to your comments yesterday. I was very busy preparing slides for a talk I gave today. I will look at the PR now.

@Chris Henson @Fabrizio Montesi: I believe I have now addressed all of your comments, except the issue with naming. I am currently using the name LTSCat as @Chris Henson suggested.

I defined the category exactly as in Winskel and Nielsen, using the lifting of the transition relation to Option Label.

Thanks for your reviews and thanks for being patient as I get used to Lean conventions :slight_smile:

I think there is also a deeper question to answer: what is the right category of LTSs? Should the labels be fixed or not? It feels bit weird to consider morphisms between LTSs with different label sets but I kind of see the motivation for it.
But in any case, the one from Winskel and Nielsen is a good start as it is (seemingly) more general than the other two.
Great! I have a couples of reviews pending but I will take another look soon.

Ayberk Tosun said:

I think there is also a deeper question to answer: what is the right category of LTSs?

I would find it very unsurprising for there to be multiple formulations for different purposes. For instance for just simply typed lambda calculi, I can think of at least four reasonable distinct categorical formulations for different use cases.

I would find it very unsurprising for there to be multiple formulations for different purposes.

I would find it surprising for all these different notions to have the name “LTS” though. Ideally, there should not be competing candidates as to what a morphism of LTSs should be. For example, automata, LTSs, and directed graphs are all similar in terms of their defining data, but they are distinguished by their notions of equivalence.

My favourite example of this from mathematics is the following three concepts: frame, locale, and complete Heyting algebra. They are _exactly_ the same thing as long as no mention to morphisms is made but they have very different attitudes when considered as objects in different categories.

Actually, this is exactly what I wanted to understand in the context of LTSs, which is why I started looking into categories of LTSs. I came to CSLib to find if there is a standard one so I can understand its meaning.
I am really not familiar enough with LTSs to say, I am just imagining the analogy to what I described for lambda calculi at #CSLib > Categorical Semantics @ 💬.

I think having LTSs with different label types (in the same category) and therefore label mappings is reasonable, if we have the same for states.

There is really no standard 'good choice' for labels. People choose as label type for an LTS what they're interested in observing, keeping it as abstract as possible but not too abstract: it's the usual trade-off in mathematical modelling.

Sometimes people even define different LTSs with different labels for the same states.

Re naming:

I think the current naming is weird:

structure LTSCat : Type (max u v + 1) where
  State : Type u
  Label : Type v
  lts : LTS State Label

As LTSCat makes me think of the category of LTSs, but this is just a bundled LTS.

I'd like to figure out how a consistent way to do bundling. In cslib#398, I just called it <typename>.Bundled. Could we adopt the same here (LTS.Bundled), or is it problematic?

We could either:

-- option 1
structure LTS.Bundled : Type (max u v + 1) where
  State : Type u
  Label : Type v
  lts : LTS State Label

or

-- option 2
structure LTS.Bundled : Type (max u v + 1) where
  State : Type u
  Label : Type v
  Tr : State → Label → State → Prop

Should we also have some coercions back and forth?

We're gonna have this a lot. In cslib#398, I had to bundle because something didn't work well with currying, and we do love currying otherwise.
(the rest of the PR looks pretty good now!)

I suggested that name because of it being standard in Mathlib to name the bundled type of objects of a category this way.

Are you suggesting to have both options you list above with coercions or pick one and coerce to LTS? I don't understand the motivation for this. We need the bundled type here specifically for use as a category, is there some other future use case you have in mind?

I'm suggesting to pick one.

Re future cases: in HML I had to bundle things to fit within typeclasses. It seems to me this has the potential to be a general issue, so I wouldn't be surprised if the usefulness of defining bundled variants is not confined to category theory.

As LTSCat makes me think of the category of LTSs, but this is just a bundled LTS.

I agree with this.

but also

because of it being standard in Mathlib

if this is Mathlib’s standard for algebraic structures, I think it’s best to follow that convention even if it’s not ideal.

I had to bundle because something didn't work well with currying, and we do love currying otherwise.

Also in my experience of formalizing mathematics (in Agda), I’ve had this a lot.

Let me note that there is a well-principled approach to the general question of a type equipped with some algebraic structure in MLTT: https://martinescardo.github.io/HoTT-UF-in-Agda-Lecture-Notes/HoTT-UF-Agda.html#sip. Maybe you can take inspiration from this in terms of naming.

My preference would be that in the interest of keeping the scope of cslib#391 encapsulated (which looks good now minus a few more minor issues I pointed out on the review) that we leave some of this to a follow up PR. If there are other use cases then I don't mind the LTS.Bundled name, but then it should really be in an independent import. I'd prefer to keep this isolated until we have a concrete use case where we can carefully consider if we need this bundling.

For the two options, I think I have a preference for the first, because it would be somewhat anomalous for us to refer to an LTS by its unbundled relation, right? In reviewing 391 I'd even thought of questioning that lift does this, but figured it wasn't so important if just used in this module.
